paragraphs: Unlimited Power of the Majority in the United States, and Its Consequences

The very essence of democratic government lies in the absolute sovereignty of the majority, for nothing in democratic States is able to resist it. Most of the American Constitutions have tried to increase this natural strength of the majority by artificial means. *a

a [ We observed, in examining the Federal Constitution, that the efforts of the legislators of the Union had been diametrically opposed to the present tendency. The consequence has been that the Federal government is more independent in its sphere than that of the States. But the Federal government scarcely ever interferes in anything but external affairs, and the governments of the States are in reality the authorities that direct society in America.]

Of all political institutions, the legislature is the one most easily swayed by the wishes of the majority. The Americans decided that the members of the legislature should be elected directly by the people and for a very short term. Their purpose was to subject legislators not only to the general convictions of their constituents but even to their daily passions. The members of both houses are drawn from the same class of society and are chosen in the same way. As a result, the changes in the legislative bodies are almost as rapid, and quite as irresistible, as those of a single assembly. Almost all the authority of the government has been entrusted to a legislature constituted in this way.

But while the law increased the strength of the authorities that were already strong, it weakened more and more those that were naturally weak. It deprived the representatives of the executive of all stability and independence. By subjecting them completely to the whims of the legislature, it took from them the slight influence that the nature of a democratic government might have allowed them to keep. In several States the judicial power was also placed at the discretion of the majority through election, and in all of them its very existence was made to depend on the will of the legislative authority, since the representatives were empowered to set the judges’ salaries every year.

Custom, however, has done even more than law. A practice that will in the end make all the safeguards of representative government worthless is becoming more and more common in the United States. It often happens that the electors who choose a delegate lay down a certain line of conduct for him and impose on him a number of positive obligations that he is pledged to carry out. Apart from the tumult, this amounts to the same thing as if the majority of the people held its deliberations in the marketplace.

Several other circumstances combine to make the power of the majority in America not only preponderant but irresistible. The moral authority of the majority rests partly on the idea that there is more intelligence and wisdom in a great number of men gathered together than in a single individual, and that the number of legislators matters more than their quality. In effect, the theory of equality is applied to the human mind. Human pride is thus attacked in its last refuge by a doctrine that the minority is reluctant to admit and agrees to only very slowly. Like all other powers, and perhaps more than any other, the authority of the many needs the sanction of time. At first it compels obedience by force, but its laws are not respected until they have been maintained for a long while.

The majority supposes that its right to govern society comes from its superior intelligence. This idea was brought into the United States by the first settlers. It would be enough by itself to create a free nation, and it has now merged with the customs of the people and with the small details of social life.

Under the old monarchy the French held as a maxim that the King could do no wrong, and that if he did do wrong, the blame fell on his advisers. This maxim is still a fundamental principle of the English Constitution. It was highly favorable to habits of obedience, and it allowed the subject to complain of the law without ceasing to love and honor the lawgiver. The Americans hold the same opinion about the majority.

The moral power of the majority rests on yet another principle: that the interests of the many should be preferred to those of the few. It is easy to see that the respect professed here for the rights of the majority must naturally grow or shrink according to the state of parties. When a nation is divided into several irreconcilable factions, the privilege of the majority is often disregarded, because it is intolerable to comply with its demands.

Suppose there were in America a class of citizens whom the legislating majority tried to strip of exclusive privileges they had held for ages, and to bring down from a high position to the level of the common ranks. The minority would then probably be less ready to obey the majority’s laws. But the United States was colonized by men of equal rank among themselves, and so there is as yet no natural or permanent source of conflict between the interests of its different inhabitants.

There are certain communities in which the people who make up the minority can never hope to bring the majority over to their side, because to do so they would have to give up the very point in dispute between them. Thus an aristocracy can never become a majority while it keeps its exclusive privileges, and it cannot give up its privileges without ceasing to be an aristocracy.

In the United States political questions cannot be posed in so general and absolute a way. All parties are willing to recognize the rights of the majority, because all hope to turn those rights to their own advantage at some future time. The majority in that country therefore exercises a prodigious actual authority and a moral influence that is scarcely less preponderant. No obstacles exist that can hinder its progress, or even slow it down, or make it heed the complaints of those it crushes along its path. This state of affairs is disastrous in itself and dangerous for the future.

How the Unlimited Power of the Majority Increases in America the Instability of Legislation and Administration Inherent in Democracy The Americans increase the changeableness of the laws, which is inherent in democracy, by changing the legislature every year and giving it unbounded authority. The same effect is produced on the administration. In America social improvement is pursued more energetically but less steadily than in Europe.

I have already spoken of the natural defects of democratic institutions, and every one of them grows in exact proportion to the power of the majority. Take the most obvious first. The changeableness of the laws is an evil inherent in democratic government, because it is natural for democracies to raise men to power in very rapid succession. But this evil is felt more or less strongly depending on the authority and the means of action the legislature possesses.

In America the authority exercised by the legislative bodies is supreme. Nothing prevents them from carrying out their wishes quickly and with irresistible power, and they receive new representatives every year. That is to say, the circumstances that do most to produce democratic instability, and that allow whim to be applied freely to every object in the State, are fully at work here. In keeping with this, America today is the country in the world where laws last the shortest time. Almost all the American constitutions have been amended within thirty years, so there is not a single American State that has not changed the principles of its legislation in that time. As for the laws themselves, one glance at the archives of the various States of the Union is enough to show that in America the legislator’s activity never slackens. This is not because American democracy is naturally less stable than any other. It is because American democracy is allowed to follow its capricious inclinations in making laws. *b

b [ The legislative acts issued by the State of Massachusetts alone, from the year 1780 to the present time, already fill three stout volumes. And it must not be forgotten that the collection I mean was published in 1823, when many old laws that had fallen out of use were left out. The State of Massachusetts, which is no more populous than a department of France, may be considered the most stable, the most consistent and the most sagacious in its undertakings of the whole Union.]

The omnipotence of the majority, and the rapid as well as absolute way its decisions are carried out in the United States, not only makes the law unstable. It has the same influence on the execution of the law and on the conduct of the public administration. The majority is the only power that it is important to court, so all its projects are taken up with the greatest ardor. But as soon as its attention is distracted, all this ardor dies away. In the free States of Europe, by contrast, the administration is both independent and secure, so the projects of the legislature are carried out even when its immediate attention is directed to other matters.

In America certain improvements are undertaken with much more zeal and activity than elsewhere. In Europe the same ends are advanced with much less social effort, but that effort is applied more continuously.

Some years ago several pious individuals set out to improve the condition of the prisons. The public was stirred by what they reported, and reforming criminals became a very popular cause. New prisons were built, and for the first time the idea of reforming the offender as well as punishing him became part of prison discipline. But this happy change, in which the public had taken so hearty an interest and which the efforts of citizens had irresistibly hastened, could not be completed in a moment. While the new penitentiaries were being built (and the majority wanted them finished with all possible speed), the old prisons still stood, holding a great number of offenders. These jails became more unhealthy and more corrupt as the new establishments were made more handsome and better, and the contrast is easy to understand. The majority was so busy founding the new prisons that it forgot the existing ones. Once general attention turned to a new object, the care that had been given to the old ones stopped. The beneficial rules of discipline were first relaxed and then broken. So right next to a prison that bore witness to the mild and enlightened spirit of our time, one could find dungeons that reminded the visitor of the barbarity of the Middle Ages.
Tyranny of the Majority

How the principle of the sovereignty of the people is to be understood. The impossibility of conceiving a mixed government. The sovereign power must be centered somewhere. The precautions to be taken to control its action. These precautions have not been taken in the United States. The consequences.

I hold it to be an impious and detestable maxim that, politically speaking, a people has a right to do whatever it pleases. Yet I have asserted that all authority originates in the will of the majority. Am I then contradicting myself?

A general law, which bears the name of Justice, has been made and sanctioned not only by a majority of this or that people but by a majority of mankind. The rights of every people are therefore confined within the limits of what is just. A nation may be regarded as a jury empowered to represent society at large and to apply the great and general law of justice. Should such a jury, which represents society, have more power than the society in which the laws it applies originate?

When I refuse to obey an unjust law, I do not dispute the majority’s right to command. I simply appeal from the sovereignty of the people to the sovereignty of mankind. Some have claimed that a people can never entirely overstep the boundaries of justice and reason in those affairs that are especially its own, and that full power may therefore be given without fear to the majority that represents it. But this is the language of a slave.

A majority taken collectively may be regarded as a being whose opinions, and most often whose interests, are opposed to those of another being, called a minority. If we admit that a man with absolute power may misuse it by wronging his adversaries, why should a majority not be open to the same reproach? Men do not change their character by coming together in numbers, and their patience in the face of obstacles does not grow with their awareness of their strength. *c For these reasons I can never willingly give any number of my fellow creatures the unlimited authority that I would refuse to any one of them.

c [ No one will assert that a people cannot do forcible wrong to another people. But parties may be looked on as lesser nations within a greater one, and they are strangers to each other. So if it is admitted that a nation can act tyrannically toward another nation, it cannot be denied that a party may do the same toward another party.]

I do not think it possible to combine several principles in the same government in such a way as to keep freedom and really set the principles against one another. The form of government usually called mixed has always seemed to me a mere chimera. Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as a mixed government, in the sense usually given to that term, because in every community one principle of action or another can be found that outweighs the rest. England in the last century is the example most often cited of this form of government. In fact it was an essentially aristocratic State, although it contained very powerful elements of democracy. For its laws and customs were such that the aristocracy could not fail to prevail in the end and bring the direction of public affairs under its own will. The error arose from paying too much attention to the actual struggle going on between the nobles and the people, and not considering the probable outcome of the contest, which was in reality the important point. When a community really has a mixed government, that is, when it is equally divided between two opposed principles, it must either pass through a revolution or fall into complete dissolution.

I am therefore of the opinion that one social power must always be made to predominate over the others. But I think liberty is in danger when this power meets no obstacles that might slow its course and force it to moderate its own vehemence.

Unlimited power is in itself a bad and dangerous thing. Human beings are not able to exercise it with discretion, and only God can be omnipotent, because His wisdom and His justice are always equal to His power. But no power on earth is so worthy of honor in itself, or of reverent obedience for the rights it represents, that I would agree to admit its uncontrolled and all-predominant authority. When I see the right and the means of absolute command given to a people or a king, to an aristocracy or a democracy, to a monarchy or a republic, I recognize the seed of tyranny, and I travel on to a land of more hopeful institutions.

In my opinion the main evil of the present democratic institutions of the United States does not come, as is often claimed in Europe, from their weakness, but from their overpowering strength. What alarms me most is not the excessive liberty that reigns in that country but the very inadequate safeguards against tyranny.

When an individual or a party is wronged in the United States, to whom can he turn for redress? To public opinion? Public opinion is the majority. To the legislature? It represents the majority and obeys its orders without question. To the executive power? It is appointed by the majority and remains a passive tool in its hands. The public troops are the majority under arms. The jury is the majority with the right to hear judicial cases. In certain States even the judges are elected by the majority. However unjust or absurd the wrong you complain of, you must put up with it as best you can. *d

d [ A striking instance of the excesses that the despotism of the majority can cause occurred at Baltimore in 1812. At that time the war was very popular in Baltimore. A newspaper that had taken the other side of the question aroused the anger of the inhabitants by its opposition. The crowd gathered, broke the printing presses and attacked the houses of the newspaper’s editors. The militia was called out, but no one obeyed the call. The only way to save the poor wretches threatened by the frenzy of the mob was to throw them into prison as common criminals. But even this precaution was useless. The mob gathered again during the night, and the magistrates again made a vain attempt to call out the militia. The prison was broken into, one of the editors was killed on the spot, and the others were left for dead. When the guilty parties were brought to trial, the jury acquitted them.

One day I said to an inhabitant of Pennsylvania, “Please explain to me how it happens that in a State founded by Quakers and famous for its toleration, freed Black people are not allowed to exercise civil rights. They pay taxes. Is it not fair that they should have a vote?”
“You insult us,” my informant replied, “if you imagine that our legislators could have committed so gross an act of injustice and intolerance.”
“What! Then Black people have the right to vote in this county?”
“Without the smallest doubt.”
“How does it happen, then, that at the polling place this morning I did not see a single Black person in the whole meeting?”
“This is not the fault of the law. Black people have an undisputed right to vote, but they voluntarily stay away.”
“A very pretty piece of modesty on their part!” I answered.

“Why, the truth is that they are not unwilling to vote, but they are afraid of being mistreated. In this country the law is sometimes unable to maintain its authority without the support of the majority. But in this case the majority has very strong prejudices against Black people, and the magistrates are unable to protect them in the exercise of their legal rights.”
“What! Then the majority claims the right not only to make the laws but to break the laws it has made?”]

Suppose, on the other hand, that a legislative power could be constituted so as to represent the majority without necessarily being the slave of its passions. Suppose an executive could be constituted so as to keep a certain degree of uncontrolled authority, and a judiciary so as to remain independent of the other two powers. A government would then be formed that would still be democratic without any risk of tyrannical abuse.

I do not say that tyrannical abuses often occur in America today. But I maintain that no sure barrier is set against them, and that the causes that moderate the government are to be found in the circumstances and customs of the country more than in its laws.
Effects of the Unlimited Power of the Majority on the Arbitrary Authority of American Public Officials
The liberty that American laws leave to public officials within a certain sphere, and their power.

A distinction must be drawn between tyranny and arbitrary power. Tyranny may be exercised through the law, and in that case it is not arbitrary. Arbitrary power may be exercised for the good of the community at large, and in that case it is not tyrannical. Tyranny usually uses arbitrary means, but if necessary it can rule without them.

In the United States the unbounded power of the majority favors the legal despotism of the legislature, and it equally favors the arbitrary authority of the magistrate. The majority has complete control over the law, both when it is made and when it is carried out. It has equal authority over those who hold power and over the community at large. It therefore regards public officials as its passive agents and readily entrusts the task of serving its designs to their vigilance. The details of their office and the privileges they are to enjoy are rarely defined in advance. Instead the majority treats them as a master treats servants who are always working under his eye, and whom he can direct or reprimand at any moment.

In general, American officials are far more independent than French civil officers within the sphere prescribed to them. Sometimes the popular authority even allows them to go beyond those limits. They are protected by opinion and backed by the cooperation of the majority, and so they dare to show their power in ways that astonish a European. In this way habits are formed in the heart of a free country that may one day prove fatal to its liberties.
Power Exercised by the Majority in America over Opinion

In America, when the majority has once irrevocably decided a question, all discussion ceases. The reason for this. The moral power the majority exercises over opinion. Democratic republics have taken from despotism its physical instruments. Their despotism rules the minds of men.

It is by examining how public opinion shows itself in the United States that we see clearly how far the power of the majority surpasses all the powers we know in Europe. Intellectual principles exert an influence so invisible, and often so impossible to measure, that they defeat the efforts of oppression. At the present time the most absolute monarchs in Europe cannot stop certain ideas opposed to their authority from circulating secretly throughout their dominions, and even in their courts. This is not so in America. As long as the majority is undecided, discussion goes on. But as soon as its decision is irrevocably pronounced, a submissive silence follows, and the friends of the measure and its opponents alike agree that it is right. The reason is perfectly clear. No monarch is so absolute that he can gather all the powers of society into his own hands and overcome all opposition with the energy of a majority that has the right to make and carry out the laws.

The authority of a king is purely physical. It controls the actions of the subject without subduing his private will. But the majority has a power that is both physical and moral at once. It acts on the will as well as on the actions of men, and it suppresses not only all contest but all controversy. I know of no country in which there is so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as in America. In any constitutional state in Europe, every kind of religious and political theory may be advocated and spread abroad. No country in Europe is so subdued by a single authority that it lacks citizens ready to shield from the consequences of his boldness the man who raises his voice for the truth. If he is unfortunate enough to live under an absolute government, the people are on his side. If he lives in a free country, he can find shelter behind the authority of the throne, should he need it. In some countries the aristocratic part of society supports him, and in others the democracy does. But in a nation with democratic institutions organized as they are in the United States, there is only one authority, one single element of strength and success, and nothing beyond it.

In America the majority raises very formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion. Within these barriers an author may write whatever he pleases, but he will regret it if he ever steps beyond them. He is not exposed to the terrors of an auto-da-fé, but he is tormented by the slights and persecutions of daily abuse. His political career is closed forever, because he has offended the only authority that can advance his success. Every kind of compensation, even that of celebrity, is refused him. Before he published his opinions, he imagined he shared them with many others. But as soon as he has declared them openly, his overbearing opponents loudly condemn him, while those who think as he does but lack the courage to say so abandon him in silence. In the end he gives way, worn down by his daily efforts, and he falls silent, as if tormented by remorse for having spoken the truth.

Chains and executioners were the crude instruments that tyranny once used. But the civilization of our age has refined the arts of despotism, which had seemed already perfected enough. The excesses of monarchical power had devised a variety of physical means of oppression. The democratic republics of the present day have made oppression as entirely a matter of the mind as the will it is meant to coerce. Under the absolute rule of a single despot, the body was attacked in order to subdue the soul, but the soul escaped the blows aimed at it and rose above the attempt. Tyranny in democratic republics takes a different course. There the body is left free, and the soul is enslaved. The sovereign can no longer say, “You shall think as I do, or die.” But he says, “You are free to think differently from me, and to keep your life, your property and all that you own. But if you choose this, you are from now on a stranger among your own people. You may keep your civil rights, but they will be useless to you, for you will never be chosen by your fellow citizens if you ask for their votes, and they will pretend to scorn you if you ask for their esteem. You will remain among men, but you will be deprived of the rights of mankind. Your fellow creatures will shun you like an unclean being, and even those who are most convinced of your innocence will abandon you too, for fear of being shunned in their turn. Go in peace! I have given you your life, but it is an existence incomparably worse than death.”

Monarchical institutions have made despotism hateful. Let us beware that democratic republics do not bring oppression back and make it less hateful and less degrading in the eyes of the many by making it still heavier for the few.

In the proudest nations of the Old World, works have been published expressly to censure the vices and mock the follies of the times. Labruyere lived in the palace of Louis XIV when he wrote his chapter on the Great, and Moliere criticized the courtiers in the very plays that were performed before the Court. But the ruling power in the United States will not be made fun of. The smallest reproach irritates its sensitivity, and the slightest joke with any foundation in truth makes it indignant. Everything, from the style of its language to the more solid virtues of its character, must be praised. No writer, whatever his eminence, can escape paying this tribute of flattery to his fellow citizens. The majority lives in the constant practice of self-praise, and there are certain truths that the Americans can learn only from strangers or from experience.

If great writers have not yet appeared in America, the reason is simply given by these facts. There can be no literary genius without freedom of opinion, and freedom of opinion does not exist in America. The Inquisition was never able to stop a vast number of anti-religious books from circulating in Spain. The empire of the majority succeeds much better in the United States, since it actually removes the wish to publish such books. There are unbelievers in America, but, to tell the truth, there is no public voice of unbelief. Some governments have tried to protect the morality of nations by banning licentious books. In the United States no one is punished for writing this sort of work, but no one is tempted to write it. This is not because all the citizens are spotless in their morals, but because the majority of the community is decent and orderly.

In these cases the advantages gained from the exercise of this power are unquestionable. I am simply discussing the nature of the power itself. This irresistible authority is a constant fact, and its wise exercise is a matter of chance.
Effects of the Tyranny of the Majority on the National Character of the Americans

The effects of the tyranny of the majority have so far been felt more in customs than in the conduct of society. They check the development of leading characters. Democratic republics organized like the United States put the practice of courting favor within the reach of the many. Proofs of this spirit in the United States. Why there is more patriotism in the people than in those who govern in its name.

The tendencies I have just mentioned are still only slightly perceptible in political society, but they are already beginning to have an unfavorable influence on the national character of the Americans. I am inclined to attribute the unusual scarcity of distinguished political figures to the ever-increasing activity of the despotism of the majority in the United States. When the American Revolution broke out, such figures appeared in great numbers, for public opinion then served not to tyrannize over individuals but to direct their efforts. Those celebrated men took a full part in the general stirring of minds common at that time. They won a high degree of personal fame, which reflected back on the nation but was by no means borrowed from it.

In absolute governments, the great nobles nearest the throne flatter the sovereign’s passions and willingly bow to his whims. But the mass of the nation does not degrade itself by servitude. It often submits from weakness, from habit or from ignorance, and sometimes from loyalty. Some nations have been known to sacrifice their own desires to those of the sovereign with pleasure and pride, and so show a kind of independence in the very act of submission. These peoples are miserable, but they are not degraded. There is a great difference between doing what one does not approve of and pretending to approve of what one does. The first is the necessary lot of a weak person, and the second suits the temper of a lackey.

In free countries, everyone is more or less called on to give his opinion on affairs of state. In democratic republics, public life is constantly mixed up with domestic affairs, the sovereign authority is accessible from every side, and its attention can almost always be caught by shouting. In such countries more people are found who play on its weaknesses and live at the expense of its passions than in absolute monarchies. This is not because men are naturally worse in these States than elsewhere, but because the temptation is both stronger and easier to reach. The result is a far more widespread debasement of the character of citizens.

Democratic republics spread the practice of currying favor with the many, and they bring it into a greater number of classes at once. This is one of the most serious reproaches that can be made against them. It is especially true in democratic States organized on the principles of the American republics, where the authority of the majority is so absolute and so irresistible that a man must give up his rights as a citizen, and almost renounce his quality as a human being, if he means to stray from the track it lays down.

In the immense crowd that throngs the avenues to power in the United States, I found very few men who showed any of that manly candor and that vigorous independence of opinion that often distinguished the Americans in former times, and that is the leading feature of distinguished characters wherever they are found. At first sight it seems as if all American minds were formed on one model, so closely do they agree in their way of judging. A stranger does sometimes meet Americans who dissent from these rigid formulas. They are men who deplore the defects of the laws and the changeableness and ignorance of democracy. They even go so far as to notice the evil tendencies that damage the national character, and to point out remedies that might be applied. But no one is there to hear these things except you, and you, to whom these private reflections are confided, are a stranger and a bird of passage. They are very ready to tell you truths that are useless to you, but in public they continue to speak a different language.

If these lines are ever read in America, I am sure of two things. First, everyone who reads them will raise his voice to condemn me. Second, very many of them will acquit me in the depths of their conscience.

I have heard talk of patriotism in the United States, and it is a virtue that can be found among the people, but never among the leaders of the people. This can be explained by analogy. Despotism debases the oppressed much more than the oppressor. In absolute monarchies the king often has great virtues, but the courtiers are invariably servile. It is true that American courtiers do not say “Sire” or “Your Majesty,” a distinction without a difference. They are forever talking about the natural intelligence of the populace they serve. They do not debate which of their master’s virtues is most worthy of admiration, for they assure him that he possesses every virtue under heaven without having acquired them, or without caring to acquire them. They do not give him their daughters and wives to be raised at his pleasure to the rank of his concubines, but by sacrificing their opinions they prostitute themselves. Moralists and philosophers in America are not obliged to hide their opinions under the veil of allegory. But before they venture a harsh truth, they say, “We know that the people we are addressing is too far above all the weaknesses of human nature to lose its temper for an instant. We would not speak this way if we were not speaking to men whose virtues and intelligence make them more worthy of freedom than all the rest of the world.” The flatterers of Louis XIV could not have flattered more skillfully. For my part, I am convinced that in all governments, whatever their nature, servility will cower before force and flattery will cling to power. The only way to keep men from degrading themselves is to give no one that unlimited authority which is the surest way of debasing them.
The Greatest Dangers of the American Republics Come from the Unlimited Power of the Majority

Democratic republics are liable to perish from a misuse of their power and not from weakness. The governments of the American republics are more centralized and more energetic than those of the monarchies of Europe. The dangers that result from this. The opinions of Hamilton and Jefferson on this point.

Governments usually fall victim either to weakness or to tyranny. In the first case their power slips away from them. In the second it is wrested from their grasp. Many observers who have witnessed the anarchy of democratic States have imagined that the government of those States was naturally weak and powerless. The truth is that once hostilities have begun between parties, the government loses its control over society. But I do not think that a democratic power is naturally without force or without resources. Rather, it is almost always through the abuse of its force and the misuse of its resources that a democratic government fails. Anarchy is almost always produced by its tyranny or its mistakes, not by its lack of strength.

It is important not to confuse stability with force, or the greatness of a thing with its duration. In democratic republics, the power that directs *e society is not stable, for it often changes hands and takes a new direction. But whichever way it turns, its force is almost irresistible. The governments of the American republics seem to me as centralized as those of the absolute monarchies of Europe, and more energetic than they are. I therefore do not imagine that they will perish from weakness. *f
e [ This power may be centered in an assembly, in which case it will be strong without being stable. Or it may be centered in an individual, in which case it will be less strong but more stable.]
